opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I don't think of them as two separate things anymore. Early on I did. I thought there was a "learning phase" and then an "execution phase," and you graduate from one to the other. At a startup, especially one working on something as frontier as AI for mathematics, that split just doesn't hold up. You learn *by* executing. Every time we ship something, a new model checkpoint, a new piece of infrastructure, a result on a benchmark, reality tells us something we couldn't have figured out by sitting and thinking.

The pressure is real, though. You feel the clock all the time. The field moves incredibly fast, and other teams are working on adjacent problems. There's a temptation to just sprint and never look up. What I try to do, and I'm not always good at it, is protect a little space for reflection. After a big push, the team sits down and asks: what did we actually learn? Not just what we built, but what surprised us, what assumption turned out to be wrong.

Coming from a math background helps here, I think. In math research you get used to being stuck for a long time, and you learn that being stuck is information too. A failed proof attempt tells you where the real difficulty is. I try to bring that attitude into the company. A failed experiment isn't wasted time if you extract the lesson from it.

The other thing is that I've had to get comfortable learning things I never expected to: hiring, fundraising, managing people who are much more senior than me in certain areas. For those, I lean a lot on asking for help. I'm not shy about calling someone who has done it before and saying, "I have no idea how to do this, can you walk me through how you thought about it?" That compresses the learning curve a lot.

So I'd say the pressure to execute is actually what forces the learning to be efficient. If we had unlimited time, I'd probably read every paper and overthink every decision. The urgency makes you prioritize what you really need to understand right now and what can wait.

r001.rationale: The response says the team learns by executing and that urgency makes learning more efficient; it does not say more execution leaves less time to learn.

r002.rationale: The response mentions pressure and the temptation to sprint without reflection, but does not identify anxiety about executing quickly as a potential cause of mistakes in the startup’s strategic direction.

fable-5.1.text:
I don't think of them as opposed, honestly. At Axiom the pressure to execute is real, but almost everything we're doing hasn't been done before, so execution itself is learning. If we knew exactly how to build an AI that proves theorems and writes verified code, there would be no startup here.

What I try to protect is the direction of the learning. It's easy to learn a lot of small, local things very fast, like which infrastructure breaks, which hiring channel works, and feel busy without understanding the problem any better. So I force myself, and the team, to keep asking the fundamental question: are we getting closer to the thing we actually set out to prove? For us that's whether formal reasoning can become the backbone of trustworthy AI. If a week of frantic execution didn't move our understanding of that, it was wasted even if it shipped something.

My background helps a bit here. In mathematics you're trained to sit with a problem for a long time without visible progress, and then compress years of understanding into a few lines. In a startup, the rhythm is reversed, you have to show visible progress constantly. The discipline I'm learning is to hold both: ship daily, but reserve real time, usually mornings, for reading papers, talking to the researchers, and thinking slowly. If I don't schedule that, the urgent always eats the important.

And the last thing, I rely on the team. I'm the youngest person in a lot of rooms I'm in, and I'm surrounded by people who have spent decades on Lean, on type theory, on training models. Learning from them quickly is itself a form of execution. The best decision I can make in a day is often just asking the right question of the right person.

r001.rationale: She says to ship daily while reserving time for slow learning, and that urgent work eats that time if she does not schedule it.

r002.rationale: She warns that frantic execution may fail to advance understanding, but does not say anxiety about executing quickly can cause strategic-direction mistakes.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to make learning part of execution, rather than something you do before you execute. You’ll rarely have all the information you want at a startup. So you have to ask: What do we believe, what’s the biggest uncertainty, and what can we do this week to test it?

The tension is that moving quickly can feel productive even when you’re not learning anything. I try to distinguish between getting something out the door and getting evidence that changes our next decision. Sometimes a conversation with a customer is more valuable than another week of building.

And I think you need room to reflect. If you’re constantly executing without asking what worked and what didn’t, you can repeat the same mistake faster. The goal is a short loop: act, learn, adjust.

r001.rationale: The response says learning should be part of execution and warns that constant execution without reflection can repeat mistakes, but it does not state that more time executing leaves less time to learn.

r002.rationale: The response notes that moving quickly can feel productive without producing learning, but it does not identify anxiety about speed as a cause of mistakes in strategic direction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to make learning part of execution, rather than treating them as competing priorities. When you’re uncertain, moving quickly should mean finding the smallest thing you can do to test an assumption, getting feedback, and adjusting. It doesn’t necessarily mean committing to a big plan faster.

The pressure becomes unhealthy when you’re so focused on producing something that you stop asking whether it’s the right thing. So I try to keep those two questions together: What can we get done this week, and what do we need to learn from it? Ideally, the work answers both.

r001.rationale: The response says learning should be part of execution and asks what the work can teach. It does not state that spending more time executing leaves less time to learn.

r002.rationale: The response says pressure to produce can make the team stop asking whether it is doing the right thing, identifying a risk to the startup’s strategic direction.
